doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Going to Sussex for a Ph.D. in American Studies
summary: Interest in sociology of black music and McLuhan led him to Sussex during Vietnam; British view of the American identity.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Let me take you back for a bit. Why did you go to England to work on a Ph.D. in American Studies?

Well by that point I was really interested in the sociology of black music. We’re talking about the late ‘60s. And nobody was talking about this. And people weren’t talking about the importance of popular culture back then. Now it’s everywhere of course. But back then popular culture would have been irrelevant in the academic world. Who cares or who even knows what it is? It was Marshall McLuhan’s Understanding Media that got me started thinking about how we perceive the world and how we move through it in terms of what we hear, what we see, what we do. It’s not just a reflection of who we are but a cause of who we are. And I had all these thoughts in my head about the music and I was completely caught up in the culture of the ‘60s. And there was this interdisciplinary graduate program at Sussex University in Brighton. It was really ahead of its time. American Studies is really interdisciplinary approach using the various elements of history, sociology, psychology, literature, whatever you want, to study a larger picture. And I wanted to talk about black music in America and the politics of America and the sociology of living in America. And there were very few places where you could do that. One was Yale, which because also it was during the Vietnam War and I wasn’t unhappy about leaving the United States at the time, so that’s how I got to Sussex University.

Did the British professors — well maybe you don’t have a comparison for this, but I’m just wondering if their attitudes and philosophies about America would be significantly different than American professors?

Absolutely. Absolutely. I was stunned actually my first semester there when I took a seminar the title of which had something to do with the American identity. And I didn’t know Americans had an identity, I had no thought about an American identity. I mean I could give you a précis of the French identity or the British identity, but I always thought of America as just being chaos in a way. But the fact that they were talking about the American identity I found fascinating. And again, it partially was being able to see the forest when you got outside of the trees and I was able to look at America. I mean for example we were all consumed with the Vietnam was but when I got to England — it was shocking — discovered that it wasn’t their war, they weren’t talking about it. Yeah. And the courses that I took were very interesting and applicable to what I was concerned about. Like I had a sociology course and my takeaway from that course was to the other guy you are the other guy. And I thought that’s, you know, we’re all together in this. We’re all outsiders in some sense.
